description:
Blue-gray Gnatcatcher (Polioptila caerulea)

8 June 2016
Greenbelt Corridor Ray Roberts/Lewisville Lake FM 428 Access Area, Aubrey Branch
Denton County, Texas

A pair of Blue-gray Gnatcatchers were foraging on the trail and upon our approach took flight to the top of towering trees on either side of it. The one we managed to photograph appears to have some yellow still at the gape meaning it is likely part of this year's new crop of Blue-gray Gnatcatcher, recently fledged. Blue-gray Gnatcatcher ranges from the Southwest and eastern half of the United States to northern Central America. Mostly, it is a migratory bird and reproduces while in the US. It is a permanent resident in most of Mexico, the Gulf of Mexico coastal areas of Texas and the Gulf Coast generally to Florida thence north along the Atlantic coastal areas of Florida, Georgia and South Carolina. Its North American presence makes it an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The Greenbelt Corridor FM 428 Access Area is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

Source: "Blue-gray Gnatcatcher," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Cornell University, photographs, range map, description, resources, accessed 6.8.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Blue-gray_Gnatcatcher/id

description:
This organism is about the size of a softball and has blue-gray feathers on the top of its body and wings and white feathers underneath. It has a big, round belly and a long tail that it uses to flick on the ground to scare up potential food, like spiders and small insects. It has two eyes, no external ears, and a small beak for eating small insects and spiders. The organism was found by itself in a small tree on USF campus with many small branches and leaves. The weather was a little chilly, but sunny. Based on where this organism was found and its characteristics, it can be identified as a blue-gray gnatcatcher. These birds are found from southern Ontario to southern Mexico, spanning from the east to the west of the United States. Their habitats range from moist areas and trees on the east coast and shorter woodlands and shrubs on the west coast. This species belongs to Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Genus Polioptila.

description:
Taken during the Corpus Christi Christmas Bird Count on the Angelita ranch on the Nueces river. The ranch hosts a few birders each year to cover this area of the count circle with the goal of covering southwestern scrub habitat and finding lingering neotropical migrant songbirds in the riparian woods along the river.

I used Eastern Screech-Owl recording playback extensively, something I don't normally do for other types of birding. But during CBC's it's the most efficient way to find and count most birds in a small area. Some of the responses to the recording were specatular that morning! But it's important to remember that the bids are wasting their energy responding, and this technique should be used sparingly.

I saw my organism in a forest habitat.  
Blue-gray Gnatcatchers are found over most of the U.S from east mississpie to west California, a big part of Mexico, and southern parts of the U.S. 
One reference is allaboutbirds.org; they provide me with a description of the bird, ranges, characteristics, and more. 
My initial observation was the same as Inatrualist because I identified my bird using the allaboutbirds.org website, which helped me identify even using sound. 
I could identify it at the class level because I knew it was a bird; however, species was where I could locate the Blue-grey gnatcatcher.

description:
Identification: 
Class: Aves
Order: Passeriformes
a. I classified this species as a member of Aves because it has feathers. I classified this bird as a member of Order Passeriformes because it has a anisodactyl feet.
b. During the time of my observation, it was cloudy with a cool breeze. The temperature was about 68 degrees F.
c. The place of the location where I took the picture was at Sweetwater Wetlands (iNaturalist made it show up a Paines Prairie). The place consists of a large body of water with a lot of dense vegetation ranging from tall grasses to small plants sitting at the surface of the water. A bridge stretches through the wetlands that would allow visitors to walk along it. There were also other trails (and not just the bridge) that visitors could walk along. A smaller bridge runs through a small forest before you walk into the wetlands. 
d. The bird was near the smaller bridge of Sweetwater Wetlands. It was flying through the dense grasses in the small forest. Occasionally, it would be flying rapidly and focusing on something (similar to how a hummingbird sees a flower with nectar). Given its name, I think that it was because it saw a potential insect to eat. There were a few birds (not pictured) of different species in the same grasses as the bird, but overall they did not interact with one another.

description:
I wish I had gotten a better look at the underside of tail. 

COMPARISON of Black-tailed Gnatcatcher (Polioptila melanura) vrs Blue-gray Gnatcatcher
(Polioptila caerulea)

xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

Black-tailed Gnatcatcher (Polioptila melanura) Length is 10cm (4 inches). It has a strongly graduated tail (wider at end than at base) with white tips to outer tail feathers. Male has a black cap that comes down to white eye ring.
Per Ebird: "Tiny gray insectivore of scrubby areas in the southwest U.S. and northern Mexico. Breeding males show a black cap with a thin white eyering; nonbreeding males have a thin black line over the eye. Females lack any black on the head. Note tail pattern from below: mostly black with bold white spots. Prefers dry, scrubby habitats such as desert washes, where pairs flit around in the low bushes. Listen for harsh scolding calls. Compare with Blue-gray Gnatcatcher, but note Black-tailed often looks drabber brownish-gray, and has much more black on the underside of the tail."
Ebird with species description, range map and sound recordings: https://ebird.org/species/bktgna/

Xeno-canto Bird songs, sound recordings, and species range map: https://xeno-canto.org/species/Polioptila-melanura

National Geographic Field Guide to the Birds of Western North America, ed. Jon L. Dunn, 2008, pp. 304-305.

Habitat of Black-tailed Gnatcatcher: "Desert brush, ravines, dry washes, mesquites. Found in many dry, scrubby habitats. Most common in Sonoran desert with varied growth of mesquites, acacias, and paloverdes, but also found in low acacia scrub and on open flats of creosote bush.
This long-tailed little insect-eater is at home in the desert southwest, even in arid scrub and creosote bush flats where there are few other birds. Black-tailed Gnatcatchers live in pairs all year, foraging together actively in the low brush. They stay in contact with each other using a wide variety of calls; some of these calls sound suspiciously like imitations of other desert birds, such as Verdin or Black-throated Sparrow."
Audubon Guide to North American Birds https://www.audubon.org/bird-guide

xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx


Blue-gray Gnatcatcher (Polioptila caerulea) Length is 11 cm (4.25 inches). It has pure white outer tail feathers that are less graduated than Black-tailed Gnatcatcher. Male has a thin black line above white eye ring. 
Per Ebird: "A tiny, long-tailed, thin-billed songbird. Soft blue-gray above and whitish below, with a thin white eyering. Breeding males have a black band across the forehead. Forages actively for insects, often actively twitching its long tail. Can be found singly or in pairs, sometimes with mixed flocks of other songbirds, especially during migration. Two populations: Eastern birds breed in deciduous woodlands, often near water; western birds typically breed in drier, brushier habitats. Winters from the southern U.S. to northern Central America. Compare with Black-tailed Gnatcatcher, especially the tail pattern from below: Blue-gray is mostly white, with very limited black. Also very similar to Black-capped Gnatcatcher on the wintering grounds in West Mexico; Blue-gray has a higher-pitched call."
Ebird with species description, range map and sound recordings: https://ebird.org/species/buggna/

Xeno-canto Bird songs, sound recordings, and species range map: https://xeno-canto.org/species/Polioptila-caerulea

National Geographic Field Guide to the Birds of Western North America, ed. Jon L. Dunn, 2008, pp. 304-305.

Habitat of Blue-gray Gnatcatcher : In the Western U.S, it is found in "scrubby habitat, including pinyon-juniper woods, chaparral, streamside trees, oak forest. Winters in wooded or brushy areas, often near water.

description:
COMPARISON of Black-tailed Gnatcatcher (Polioptila melanura) vrs Blue-gray Gnatcatcher
(Polioptila caerulea)

xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

Black-tailed Gnatcatcher (Polioptila melanura) Length is 10cm (4 inches). It has a strongly graduated tail (wider at end than at base) with white tips to outer tail feathers. Male has a black cap that comes down to white eye ring.
Per Ebird: "Tiny gray insectivore of scrubby areas in the southwest U.S. and northern Mexico. Breeding males show a black cap with a thin white eyering; nonbreeding males have a thin black line over the eye. Females lack any black on the head. Note tail pattern from below: mostly black with bold white spots. Prefers dry, scrubby habitats such as desert washes, where pairs flit around in the low bushes. Listen for harsh scolding calls. Compare with Blue-gray Gnatcatcher, but note Black-tailed often looks drabber brownish-gray, and has much more black on the underside of the tail."

Black-tailed Gnatcatcher confirmed observation nearby: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/195318885

Ebird with species description, range map and sound recordings: https://ebird.org/species/bktgna/

Xeno-canto Bird songs, sound recordings, and species range map: https://xeno-canto.org/species/Polioptila-melanura

National Geographic Field Guide to the Birds of Western North America, ed. Jon L. Dunn, 2008, pp. 304-305.

Habitat of Black-tailed Gnatcatcher: "Desert brush, ravines, dry washes, mesquites. Found in many dry, scrubby habitats. Most common in Sonoran desert with varied growth of mesquites, acacias, and paloverdes, but also found in low acacia scrub and on open flats of creosote bush.
This long-tailed little insect-eater is at home in the desert southwest, even in arid scrub and creosote bush flats where there are few other birds. Black-tailed Gnatcatchers live in pairs all year, foraging together actively in the low brush. They stay in contact with each other using a wide variety of calls; some of these calls sound suspiciously like imitations of other desert birds, such as Verdin or Black-throated Sparrow."
Audubon Guide to North American Birds https://www.audubon.org/bird-guide

xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

COMPARED TO 

Blue-gray Gnatcatcher (Polioptila caerulea) Length is 11 cm (4.25 inches). It has pure white outer tail feathers that are less graduated than Black-tailed Gnatcatcher. Blue-gray tail is mostly pale, with very limited black on underside of tail. Male has a thin black line above white eye ring.
Per Ebird: "A tiny, long-tailed, thin-billed songbird. Soft blue-gray above and whitish below, with a thin white eyering. Breeding males have a black band across the forehead. Forages actively for insects, often actively twitching its long tail. Can be found singly or in pairs, sometimes with mixed flocks of other songbirds, especially during migration. Two populations: Eastern birds breed in deciduous woodlands, often near water; western birds typically breed in drier, brushier habitats. Winters from the southern U.S. to northern Central America. Compare with Black-tailed Gnatcatcher, especially the tail pattern from below: Blue-gray is mostly white, with very limited black. Also very similar to Black-capped Gnatcatcher on the wintering grounds in West Mexico; Blue-gray has a higher-pitched call."

description:
A solo visit to check on the Sparkleberry bushes. They're just starting to bloom, so the next 1-3 weeks should be great for hairstreaks. There were lots of lupines, pawpaws, and especially Lyreleaf Sages blooming. Butterflies were scarce but I photographed four species of moths. Variable Dancers were common; I quit photographing them after the 4th one encountered. I walked the usual trails in clockwise order, since I wanted to visit the main Sparkleberry patch first. I used my camera to take macro photographs, and after about 15 minutes of last using it, I realized that my phone was not in my pocket. I remembered where I last used it and back-tracked my path right to the phone.

Surprisingly, there were few vehicles in the parking lot at my arrival, and no mother truckers on the mound. (Did somebody from FWC or SWFWMD finally tell the mother truckers that a state preserve is not appropriate for them to run their r/c vehicles over the area?). Several people were crossing Aripeka Road to go swimming in the pond to the south. 

The weather at my arrival was sunny and 79 degrees ("feels like" 82) -- both temperatures seemed low -- with a light breeze. The weather when I left was one degree warmer, which again seemed too low. I left at 1717 after exactly 3 hours and headed home.

description: With Don Fraser; a visit to check on the status of the Sparkleberries -- they are in prime condition now. The weather at the start was sunny and 52 degrees ("feels like" 52) with calm winds. At noon, it was sunny and 72 degrees ("feels like" 72), with a light breeze; it seemed warmer than that. Because this was a visit for hairstreaks, we had 2+ hours to spend before we could reasonably expect the butterflies to come out (it really was around 1100). As a result, we walked all the trails, including "the back 40" and the road to the barn. We finished the visit with nearly an hour at the main Sparkleberry patch, where we saw 4 Great Purple Hairstreaks and one Mangrove Skipper -- we saw one White M Hairstreak and another Mangrove Skipper on "Hairstreak Hill." The Mangrove Skippers were at least one mile east of the nearest mangroves; these are the third and fourth records for the Preserve. We left at 1308.

description:
A solo visit after a job nearby, arriving at 1147. It has been probably a year since I was last here. I first walked the western trails to the end, stopping frequently. Then I headed back to the parking lot and walked the eastern portion of the park (there are no trails here) to the observation platform. Finally, I spent several minutes at the rock mound south of the parking lot, and maybe 10 more minutes along the entrance road to the park sign. Common Ground-Doves were common, with 12 (as singles or duos) seen or heard. There were HUNDREDS of small orangish moths throughout the park. I think they were mostly or entirely Garden Webworm Moths, but none has been Research Graded yet, so they could be a similar species. I kept an eye out for Western Pygmy-Blues but found none. The weather at the start was overcast (I never saw the sun while here), 86 degrees ("feels like" 97), and breezy. By the time I left, it was 88 ("feels like" 100). I left at 1328 and headed home.

These are my camera photographs, which lack a specific time and location.

description: I’ve seen some interesting debate on the subspecies for the western-most blue grey gnatcatcher subspecies outside of the southern Baja peninsula. It appears iNat follows the Birds of the World breakdown of the subspecies, with Polioptila caerulea amoenissima breeding from northern California, through central Nevada, east to Colorado, and south to the northern portion of Baja Mexico and Sonora. Originally included as a junior synonym of P. c. obscura, Grinnell (1926) described western birds outside of southern Baja as duller in colouration (approaching the eastern subspecies) with extended black base on the inner web of the outer most rectrix, and a slender bill. The divergence between of P. c. obscura and of P. c. amoenissima is also supported on a genetic level, Smith et al (2018) using 1 mitochondrial locus along along with 6 nuclear loci to assess phylogenetic relationships within amongst members of the genus Polioptila.

description: A solo visit because I had not visited this site in 6 months! The weather at the start was clear, 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), and breezy. I walked all the usual trails in the usual order. I did not see a SINGLE Neotropical migrant! They all must have left last night. Almost all of the Coastal Plain Honeycombhead plants were knocked over by Hurricane Helene and/or Hurricane Milton, but I checked most (maybe 400) flowers for Schinia flower moths, finding none. Six trees (4 Sand Pines, 1 Turkey Oak, and 1 Red Maple) were toppled by Milton, but I got around or through all of them. The windy conditions ruled out macro photography with my cellphone. From 1030-1230, I conducted a stationary watch from the southern mound, the first time in several years that I have done this (there were no Mother Truckers in the Preserve today!). I left at 1234, when the weather was sunny, 79 ("feels like" 83), and breezy. It was an absolutely delightful day to be out!

Black-tailed Gnatcatcher (Polioptila melanura) drabber brownish-gray and tail pattern from below: mostly black with some bold white spots.

Irene's Gnatcatchers (Polioptila genus) observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=7490&user_id=aparrot1

Black-tailed Gnatcatcher (Polioptila melanura) is a small, migratory bird in the Gnatcatchers and Gnatwrens (Polioptilidae) family with a length of 10cm (4 inches). It has a strongly graduated tail (wider at end than at base) with white tips to outer tail feathers. Male has a black cap that comes down to white eye ring.
Per Ebird: "Tiny gray insectivore of scrubby areas in the southwest U.S. and northern Mexico. Breeding males show a black cap with a thin white eyering; nonbreeding males have a thin black line over the eye. Females lack any black on the head. Note tail pattern from below: mostly black with bold white spots. Prefers dry, scrubby habitats such as desert washes, where pairs flit around in the low bushes. Listen for harsh scolding calls. Compare with Blue-gray Gnatcatcher, but note Black-tailed often looks drabber brownish-gray, and has much more black on the underside of the tail."

My favorite Black-tailed Gnatcatcher confirmed observations:
In-flight Closeup: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/195318885

Ebird with species description, range map and sound recordings: https://ebird.org/species/bktgna/

Xeno-canto Bird songs, sound recordings, and species range map: https://xeno-canto.org/species/Polioptila-melanura

National Geographic Field Guide to the Birds of Western North America, ed. Jon L. Dunn, 2008, pp. 304-305.

Audubon Guide to North American Birds https://www.audubon.org/bird-guide
Habitat of Black-tailed Gnatcatcher: "Desert brush, ravines, dry washes, mesquites. Found in many dry, scrubby habitats. Most common in Sonoran desert with varied growth of mesquites, acacias, and palo verdes, but also found in low acacia scrub and on open flats of creosote bush.
This long-tailed little insect-eater is at home in the desert southwest, even in arid scrub and creosote bush flats where there are few other birds. Black-tailed Gnatcatchers live in pairs all year, foraging together actively in the low brush. They stay in contact with each other using a wide variety of calls; some of these calls sound suspiciously like imitations of other desert birds, such as Verdin or Black-throated Sparrow."

Blue-gray Gnatcatcher (Polioptila caerulea) is a small, migratory bird in the Gnatcatchers and Gnatwrens (Polioptilidae) family with a length of 11 cm (4.25 inches). It has pure white outer tail feathers that are less graduated than Black-tailed Gnatcatcher. Blue-gray tail is mostly pale, with very limited black on underside of tail. Male has a thin black line above white eye ring.
Per Ebird: "A tiny, long-tailed, thin-billed songbird. Soft blue-gray above and whitish below, with a thin white eyering. Breeding males have a black band across the forehead. Forages actively for insects, often actively twitching its long tail. Can be found singly or in pairs, sometimes with mixed flocks of other songbirds, especially during migration. Two populations: Eastern birds breed in deciduous woodlands, often near water; western birds typically breed in drier, brushier habitats. Winters from the southern U.S. to northern Central America. Compare with Black-tailed Gnatcatcher, especially the tail pattern from below: Blue-gray is mostly white, with very limited black. Also very similar to Black-capped Gnatcatcher on the wintering grounds in West Mexico; Blue-gray has a higher-pitched call."

description: North Pinellas Christmas Bird Count with Mia Majetschak. While Mia covered her yard and a small park, I drove to Philippe Park (during daylight!). The temperature at the start was sunny, 55 degrees ("feels like" 53) and breezy (NNW at 12 mph). The tide was high. Mia and I met at the boat ramp around 0820 and after scoping the (nearly birdless) northwestern part of Tampa Bay, we walked the trails away from the shoreline. The damage to the park from Hurricanes Helene and Milton was relatively light, but several large oaks (decades old) were toppled. We did well here, finding owls (the incubating Great Horned Owl, a local celebrity) and three Eastern Screech-Owls that responded to our playback to attract landbirds -- I don't know that I have ever had 3 Eastern Screech-Owls respond to playback at any one spot before -- and numerous passerines, including a Western Tanager, the highlight of the CBC. (I got one headless and several out-of-focus photos. Fortunately Mia refound the tanager on 22 Dec and got definitive photos. We left at 1220 and got lunch before returning later to survey the southern half of the park.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo, a visit following our successful chase of the Dark-billed Cuckoo at Delray Beach. We made a complete circuit then returned to the concrete walkway portion, where Chuck Weber told us to look for the Golden-winged Warbler, which represents the first winter record in Florida. The weather alternated between sunny and cloudy (it had rained rather heavily just before we arrived, and was lightly sprinkling for a few minutes after we arrived), mild, and breezy. We left at 1535 and headed to Tampa, where I left my car on Friday, then Val followed me home.

Val and I had planned a three-day trip to the St. Marks/Tallahassee area this weekend. But news about the cuckoo being found on Thursday and correctly identified yesterday spread like wildfire. Serendipitously, I worked yesterday in Sarasota, and one of my co-workers was also authorized to drive the work van (I had driven the van from Tampa). My boss allowed my co-worker to drive back the van to Tampa -- saving me three hours -- and Val picked up me after the job, and we headed to Palm Beach County yesterday.
